extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, curriculum designers, and mathematics education researchers (K-12 and college instructors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for designing and judging mathematics instruction that fosters sense-making, problem-solving, enculturation into mathematical practice, and conceptual understanding rather than rote skill mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guessing and plausible reasoning (Pólya)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics depends on guessing, insight, and discovery; 'Mathematical facts are first guessed and then proved.' Students should be given opportunities to first guess and then prove mathematical facts at an appropriate level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents Pólya's epistemology: proofs are discovered by plausible reasoning. Pedagogically, this implies designing problems and activities that allow students to conjecture, test, and refine guesses before formal proof; the text repeatedly argues that learning should mirror this discovery process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide students with a sense of the discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics instruction should provide students with a sense of the discipline -- a sense of its scope, power, uses, and history. It should give them a sense of what mathematics is and how it is done, at a level appropriate for the students to experience and understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should aim not merely to transmit procedures but to convey why mathematics matters, its applications, historical development, and intellectual character so students value and feel confident about doing mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction aimed at conceptual understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should be aimed at conceptual understanding rather than at mere mechanical skills, and at developing in students the ability to apply the subject matter they have studied with flexibility and resourcefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor pedagogies and tasks that build deep ideas (e.g., understanding multiplicative structure) over drill of isolated algorithms. The chapter criticizes curricula that slice content into bite-sized techniques divorced from understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a broad range of problem types (exercises to open-ended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics instruction should provide students the opportunity to explore a broad range of problems and problem situations, ranging from exercises to open-ended problems and exploratory situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classrooms should include routine practice and genuinely open-ended or investigative tasks so students experience both skill-building and sense-making/problem discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a broad range of approaches and techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should provide students with a broad range of approaches and techniques (ranging from the straightforward application of the appropriate algorithmic methods to the use of approximation methods, various modeling techniques, and the use of heuristic problem solving strategies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage multiple solution strategies (exact algorithms, approximation, heuristics, modeling) and teach when each is appropriate; avoid constraining students to a single sanctioned method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a mathematical point of view / disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics instruction should help students to develop what might be called a 'mathematical point of view' -- a predilection to analyze and understand, to perceive structure and structural relationships, to see how things fit together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster habits such as quantifying, modeling, seeing contexts as mathematical problems (examples: Pollak's cactus estimation and checkout lane optimization). This is about attitudes/dispositions as much as skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop analytical skills and extended reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should help students develop their analytical skills, and the ability to reason in extended chains of argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize tasks that require multi-step reasoning and constructing longer arguments rather than only short procedural steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enculturation / socialization into community of practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning is a process of socialization/enculturation: students develop mathematical habits, values, and points of view through participation in a community of practice (apprenticeship, interaction with peers and experts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design classroom environments that mirror authentic mathematical communities (apprenticeship, situated practice), where norms, language, and perspectives are transmitted through social interaction (Lave, Resnick, examples of tailors' apprenticeship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning as constructive (not absorptive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research shows learning proceeds through construction, not absorption; learners actively construct understanding rather than passively absorb facts and procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional design should present opportunities for learners to build and test their own mental models and revise misconceptions, rather than treating knowledge as discrete chunks to be filled into passive minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face validity / authentic problem contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems should have plausibility and face validity; avoid contrived examples where realistic context is 'window dressing' for contrived numbers or unrepresentative scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critique of Milne's problem set shows that contrived numbers and artificial contexts undermine meaningfulness. Prefer realistic, believable settings or tasks where context plays a real role in problem structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage multiple solution methods and mathematical flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be exposed to and encouraged to use multiple legitimate methods for solving problems; curricula should not sanction only a single method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issue exemplified by mental arithmetic responses to Milne's problem: several mental strategies are equally valid. Classroom practice should validate alternative strategies and promote flexible thinking (mental economy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rote memorization and passive rule-following
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should not reinforce beliefs that learning mathematics is mostly memorizing or that doing mathematics is merely following rules provided by authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites surveys showing many students believe mathematics is memorization. Effective instruction counters this by requiring sense-making, open problem solving, and student initiative rather than passive rule application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as science of patterns; emphasize process
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is described as 'the science of patterns' emphasizing processes such as observing patterns, testing conjectures, estimation, modeling, abstraction, optimization, logical analysis, and inference from data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift emphasis from only content coverage to engagement with mathematical modes of thought and processes that develop transferable mathematical power (e.g., modeling and abstraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical/experimental methods in mathematical inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Although mathematics relies on logic as its standard of truth, it also employs observation, simulation, and experimentation as means of discovering truth; mathematical practice can be quasi-empirical (Lakatos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include activities that use data, simulation, and exploratory experiments to motivate conjectures and guide the development of definitions and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote collaboration and joint problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaboration is valuable: it can increase efficiency, sustain interest, combine complementary skills, and raise the quality of work; collaboration involves explaining, false starts, personality interaction, and shared effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage co-authorship-like activities, group problem solving, and peer interaction as central classroom practices; design tasks that require or benefit from collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach components of mathematical practice (language, norms, significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical practice includes understanding the language of practice, currently accepted results, important questions, valid methods of reasoning, and metamathematical views including criteria of significance and elegance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyondprocedural skills, instruction should acquaint students with disciplinary norms: how mathematicians communicate, judge significance, select problems, and what counts as convincing reasoning or elegant solutions (Kitcher/Greeno summary).
